title: Redwood Console: Tracing + Request Logs Debugging Demo
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a console walkthrough focused on tracing, error analysis, and request logs to demonstrate debugging flows for a healthcare customer. Customer has strict security and retention requirements; asked about SOC2, KMS, VPC/private, RBAC, and ability to run live replays against Dedicated capacity. Agreed next steps for SOC2 docs, sandbox project, and replay setup.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-05
Time: 15:30 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Aisha (Redwood AE), Jonas (Redwood SE), Marta (CS), Daniel (CTO, Nimbus), Priya (SRE), Laura (Security), Mike (Product)

Summary: quick walkthrough of Redwood Console focusing on tracing, error analysis, and request logs. Demoed live trace view, stack traces for inference errors, request-logs replay, and how to attach traces to model rollouts / canary configs. Discussed security (SOC2, KMS, VPC) and Dedicated trial for benchmarking.

[00:00] Aisha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Aisha, AE on the account. With me is Jonas from our SE team, he'll drive the console demo. Marta's here for any billing or CS questions.
[00:18] Daniel: Thanks, Aisha. Quick context — Nimbus runs a patient triage assistant in prod. We're seeing intermittent hallucinations and some timeouts during peak hours. Want to see how you help us debug and keep PII safe.
[00:32] Aisha: Totally, that's exactly what we'll cover — tracing to see per-request spans, error analysis to find root causes, and request logs + replay for deterministic repros. Jonas?
[00:40] Jonas: Yeah, jumping in. I'm going to share my screen. Sorry if the screen share lags a bit — connection's fine on my end.
[01:05] [screen share starts] Jonas: Okay first thing — the console home, you can see recent routes and models, we'll click into the 'patient-triage' route. Notice the trace rate and error spike last Tuesday.
[01:27] Priya: That spike aligns with our midnight ET batch and the new model rollout. We pushed a quantized variant for cost. Could that be related?
[01:38] Jonas: Possibly — quantization can change failure modes slightly; also kernel selection changes on certain GPUs. The trace view shows per-token latencies and a breakdown by kernel. Here you can filter by model variant, region, and hardware.
[02:05] Laura: Quick security question — when you show request logs, what fields are stored and for how long? We need to redact PHI.
[02:16] Marta: I can cover retention and redaction settings after the demo, but short answer: request logs store request/response metadata and tokenized outputs by default, retention configurable, and we support on-the-fly redaction rules and masks. Also we integrate with KMS for envelope encryption.
[02:35] Jonas: Back to tracing — each trace has spans like 'routing', 'inference', 'post-processing'. You can open a span and see the request payload, kernel selection, and KV cache hit rate. Here's an error span marked 'model-oom' — shows memory pressure.
[03:05] Daniel: The 'model-oom' label — is that from your runtime or upstream model?
[03:12] Jonas: It's from the runtime; we instrument the runtime to surface OOM, kernel fallback events, and quantization warnings. Sometimes you'll see fallback to CPU or smaller batch sizes — that's in the trace metadata.
[03:35] [00:03:50] Jonas: I want to highlight the error analysis panel — it aggregates similar errors, shows a sample of failed requests, and links to the exact request-log entry. You can also open a side-by-side diff of two responses to see where hallucination diverged.
[04:05] Mike: Side-by-side diff sounds useful. Does it show token alignment?
[04:11] Jonas: Yes, token-level diff and a confidence/score estimate per segment. It's approximate — we use heuristics, so sometimes the alignment is slightly off (transcription note: tokenization heuristics can differ).
[04:36] Priya: About request-logs replay — can we replay in our Dedicated sandbox, with the same model variant and hardware? We don't want to run replays in prod.
[04:50] Jonas: Absolutely. We support replay to a sandbox project, and you can pin model version, hardware tier, and quantization profile. For Dedicated customers you can request reserved capacity for replays to ensure consistent latency.
[05:10] Daniel: Good. We need to replicate the exact sequence that caused hallucinations. How deterministic is replay?
[05:18] Jonas: Mostly deterministic for same model binary and same random seeds — we persist RNG seeds in the trace metadata so you can reproduce sampling. Non-determinism can come from external tools or if you call external tools in a function call, but for straight generation it's high.
[05:45] Laura: On the redaction piece — can redaction be applied pre-ingest? We can't have PHI land in plaintext in logs.
[05:54] Marta: Yes, we have pre-ingest redaction rules and client-side redaction SDK hooks. You can set rules to redact PHI patterns, PII, or custom regex. We also support token-level masking and immediate hashing before logs persist.
[06:17] [06:20] Jonas: Now I'll demo a debugging flow — open trace for a failed request, expand inference span, see model variant was 'gptx-1-q4' and kernel fallback to CPU at step 24, which coincides with an OOM. Then I click 'Open request log' and we get the full request and response.
[06:45] Daniel: That kernel fallback — would that increase latency significantly? We saw 2-3x latency on the spike.
[06:52] Jonas: Yes, fallback to CPU or smaller batch reduces throughput and increases latency. In the trace you can see batch sizes drop from 8 to 1 mid-span. That aligns with your spike.
[07:20] Priya: Any quick mitigation? Auto-fallback is important but can we set a policy to fail-fast instead of fallback? We prefer to return an error than a slow response for some endpoints.
[07:32] Jonas: Yes, routing and fallback policies are configurable per route. We showed a canary/failover policy earlier — you can set 'fail-fast' or 'fallback-to-smaller-batch' or 'route-to-hosted'. We'll demo the policy UI in a sec.
[07:50] [08:05] Jonas: Switching to request logs — search by correlation ID, user ID, or time range. You can also filter logs by response code, model variant, or kernel event. Here's a log entry; note some fields redacted per the org policy.
[08:35] Priya: How long are these request logs retained by default? We need 90-day retention for audit but with stricter redaction.
[08:44] Marta: Default is 30 days for hosted, but we support custom retention up to configured limits for Dedicated / Private. For Nimbus Health we can map retention windows and SSO-based access controls.
[09:05] Laura: KMS — where does the key live? We need an HSM-backed key, not Redwood-managed.
[09:13] Marta: You can bring-your-own key (BYOK) integrated with customer-managed KMS/HSM. We only store envelopes; full private key material can be kept in your KMS.
[09:28] [09:30] Jonas: back to debugging — near the top right there's a 'replay' button on the request-log entry. I click it, choose 'sandbox-dedicated', pin the model and hardware, hit replay. You get a replay job with its own trace id.
[09:52] Daniel: Can replay jobs be rate limited? We don't want large replays to affect other teams.
[09:58] Jonas: Yeah you can set concurrency and throughput caps per sandbox or per team. Replays are queued against capacity and you can schedule them off-peak.
[10:20] Priya: For HIPAA compliance, we need audit logs showing who accessed what. Does the console include audit trails for replay actions?
[10:30] Marta: Yes, every action (replay, trace view, redaction rule change) is auditable with user identity from SSO and timestamp. We also stream audit logs to your SIEM.
[10:45] Mike: Question on costs — if we run replays frequently to debug, what's the unit cost?
[10:52] Aisha: Replays are metered as inference units based on tokens and hardware time; Dedicated trial pricing can be arranged for benchmarking. We'll include a cost estimate in the follow-up.
[11:10] Jonas: I'm going to show the error aggregation page — it groups by signature and shows sample diffs. You can pin a signature to a test set and add it to a regression monitor. If future deploys increase that signature rate, you get alerts.
[11:40] Daniel: That would help with our rollout gating. We want to fail deployments if hallucination rate increases by >2%.
[11:48] Jonas: You can set thresholds and attach auto-rollback policies. The console also surfaces per-prompt eval results if you upload labeled prompts.
[12:05] [12:15] Jonas: small demo glitch, my screen froze for a sec — sorry about that.
[12:25] Priya: no problem, still following.
[12:32] Jonas: Next, the tracing timeline — this is helpful to find correlated infra events. For example, I can overlay GPU utilization, network latency, and trace errors. You can see here a network blip at 02:03 that coincides with a spike.
[12:55] Laura: Do those overlays require infra integrations?
[13:00] Jonas: We have integrations for Prometheus, Datadog, and CloudWatch. You can push metrics or pull them in; overlays are a first-class feature.
[13:20] Daniel: If we use Private deployment, do these integrations still work?
[13:27] Jonas: Yes, for Private you can configure connectors to your telemetry stack. For air-gapped setups we provide agents that push metrics to your on-prem systems.
[13:45] Marta: Also note RBAC — you can limit who can run replays or view raw request logs. That ties to your SSO groups.
[13:58] Priya: That addresses a lot of our concerns. A quick question on retention: can we keep tokenized outputs for a short window (7 days) but longer metadata for 90 days?
[14:10] Marta: Yes, retention policies are field-level. You can keep metadata for 90 days and scrub token outputs after 7 days.
[14:28] Mike: For benchmarking — do you support deterministic playback across different hardware types? We want to compare latency on A100 vs H100.
[14:38] Jonas: Yes, replay jobs can target specific hardware. We log kernel selection and runtime telemetry so you can compare per-token latency across hardware. One caveat: some optimizations are hardware-specific so results may not be identical, but differences are measurable.
[15:05] Daniel: Good. Timeline and success criteria — we want to decide by end of November whether to run a pilot. Our success criteria: gotta show <200ms p95 and <2% hallucination regression during the POC.
[15:20] Aisha: Noted. We'll run a Dedicated trial, do replay-based benchmarks, and provide a cost/latency report.
[15:35] [15:40] Aisha: Quick call-out — security pack and SOC2 docs. Marta, will you attach the SOC2 pdf and BYOK integration guide?
[15:48] Marta: Yes, I'll include SOC2, ISO summary, and a short BYOK/HSM integration guide in the follow-up.
[16:02] Priya: About data residency — some PHI must stay in our region. Does Redwood support region-locked logging?
[16:12] Jonas: For Hosted we have region options; Dedicated and Private give you full control of region and VPC. For strict residency, Private or Dedicated is recommended.
[16:30] Laura: Also need proof of encryption-in-transit and at-rest for the POC paperwork.
[16:38] Marta: We'll include a short security checklist with encryption details.
[16:55] Jonas: Wrapping up the demo — I'll show a sample replay job finishing. You get a trace id, snapshot of environment, and side-by-side diff between original and replay.
[17:10] Daniel: Nice. A few objections on cost: our finance team is wary of sustained Dedicated pricing. Can we start with Hosted and move to Dedicated later?
[17:20] Aisha: Absolutely. Many customers start Hosted for experimentation, then transition to Dedicated for consistent throughput. We can design the POC to start Hosted with a small Dedicated sandbox for replays.
[17:40] Mike: Who typically owns the replay setup on your side vs ours?
[17:45] Jonas: We can provision the sandbox and run initial replays, but for production benchmarking we'd hand over runbooks to your SREs. We'll collaborate on the runs.
[18:00] [18:05] Priya: Any limits on number of concurrent replays?
[18:10] Jonas: Limits depend on capacity; in Dedicated you can reserve concurrency. For Hosted, replays compete with production so we recommend sandbox Dedicated for heavy replays.
[18:30] Laura: One more: can we enforce redaction rules per team? We want different teams to have different redaction levels.
[18:40] Marta: Yes, redaction policies can be scoped per route or per team and enforced at ingest with auditability.
[19:00] Aisha: Great — let's move to open Q&A.
[19:10] Daniel: Who will be our main contacts for the pilot?
[19:15] Aisha: I'll be your AE, Jonas will be SE lead, Marta on CS/security. We'll include people in the follow-up.
[19:28] Mike: Could you also include a sample runbook for replay steps?
[19:33] Jonas: I'll attach a step-by-step runbook and a short script to export and anonymize logs.
[19:45] Priya: For the POC we'll need ~2 weeks of replays and daily syncs during the run. Is that reasonable?
[19:52] Aisha: Yes, we can do a 2-week pilot. We'll put calendar invites in the follow-up.
[20:05] [20:10] Aisha: Ok recap: Redwood to share SOC2/docs, SE to provision sandbox and run sample replays, Nimbus to share redaction rules, schedule benchmark session. Any final questions?
[20:23] Daniel: No, thanks, that covers it.
[20:28] Laura: Thanks all.
[20:35] Aisha: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with notes and docs.
[20:40] [call ends]
